//: The single source of truth for what riprap wires. Both riprap's CI and
bin/riprap verify read this file, so the checker cannot drift from the wiring.
Every command here runs from the plugin, but only session-start does its work
there. The guardrail hooks are dispatched by run-payload-hook, which execs the
real script out of the project at bin/hooks/riprap/claude/ — and exits 0 in
silence if the project never ran /riprap:install, so this plugin is inert in
repositories that do not use it.
The guardrail scripts live in the project rather than here, and that is
deliberate. They share pattern libraries with the git hooks, which run for
every developer on the team — including ones who never installed this plugin.
A library living in a version-stamped, user-scoped plugin cache would simply
be missing for half of them. One rule definition, two enforcers, both
reachable from a plain clone.
lint-example.sh is deliberately absent: it is an inert template, and wiring a
rule that never fires teaches people to ignore the wiring.
No single event covers every moment the handoff rule cares about, so it is
wired to several: PreCompact is the only warning that context is about to be
lost, and it is the one event that cannot say anything to the model — it can
only block, and blocking a compaction that is already necessary wedges the
session. So it writes to disk, and SessionStart on `compact` is what points
the next context at what it wrote. SessionEnd does the same, as a last-resort
net for a session that never went through PreCompact at all. PostToolUse on
ExitPlanMode asks for the first handoff once a plan exists to write one from,
and Stop holds the turn open once whenever the tree has moved past what was last
written.
Two of these block rather than ask, in different ways. PreToolUse on
ScheduleWakeup, CronCreate, Workflow, RemoteTrigger and a backgrounded Agent/Task
refuses the call when no handoff exists yet for the branch -- except a
ScheduleWakeup that is itself ending a loop, or a foreground Agent/Task dispatch,
neither of which is unattended in the sense that matters here. A session about to
become unattended cannot be asked again once it is, so refusing the call is the
only mechanism that can still work. Stop blocks the turn from ending, once, with
decision:block: the long-standing Stop contract, which old and current Claude
Code releases alike deliver to the model, where the advisory hookSpecificOutput
it used to send was dropped in silence by every release before 2.1.163. The
price is that the user sees each block labelled a Stop hook error, as for any
Stop block; nothing in the payload says which release is running, so the form
every release delivers wins over the quieter one only some do. It never blocks
a turn some Stop hook already continued (stop_hook_active), nor one whose
payload does not say, so it cannot loop; nor a turn in plan mode, where the
model may not make the edit it would ask for. The rest only ask, because
nothing else here can compel a model to write anything.
SessionStart matches `resume` and `fork` as well. Those are not new features —
they are two of the five documented matcher values, and omitting them meant a
resumed session received no router at all, which is the single moment a handoff
is most worth surfacing.
Every hook that reads a shell command -- the destructive-command blocker, the
merge gate, secret hygiene and the worktree boundary -- is registered under all
three tools that run one: Bash, PowerShell (the primary shell on Windows) and
Monitor. Each carries its command in tool_input.command, and a matcher of exact
names is the form the hooks reference documents for them (Bash|PowerShell).
Registered for Bash alone, each hook was blind to the same command run through
either of the other two, which is where an agent refused in Bash can go next.
The commands these hooks look for are spelled the same in either shell, so they
need no PowerShell grammar of their own beyond what lib/shell-tools.sh does for
all four: joining its backtick line continuations, reading its backtick escapes,
taking a backslash as a path separator, and dropping its comments.
The merge gate is wired a second time, under a matcher of its own for the GitHub
MCP server's merge_pull_request and enable_pr_auto_merge, which never reached it
while it was registered for shell commands alone. The MCP server's name is whatever
an installation called it, and a plugin-bundled server is named
mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>, so the matcher takes any prefix. A matcher holding
anything but letters, digits, _, -, spaces, commas and | is a regular expression
tested unanchored, which is why each alternative carries its own ^ and $: without
them, any tool whose name merely contained merge_pull_request would be sent here.
bin/tests/test-plugin-hooks.sh evaluates the matchers by that rule.
